title: A New Bill Wants to Kill the H-1B Green Card Pipeline. Every Indian Worker in America Should Read It.
excerpt: Rep. Chip Roy's American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act would end dual intent, eliminate OPT, and cut the visa to two years. If it passes, the rules of the game change entirely.
body:
A Republican congressman from Texas wants to turn the H-1B visa into something it was never designed to be: a round-trip ticket.

Representative Chip Roy introduced the American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act on June 4, a bill that would sever the H-1B visa's decades-old connection to permanent residency in the United States. If enacted, it would bar H-1B holders from using the visa as a stepping stone to a green card — a pathway that hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals have relied on to build lives, careers, and families in America.

The bill goes further than any recent legislative effort to reshape the programme. It would slash the visa's maximum duration from six years to two, eliminate the Optional Practical Training programme that lets international graduates work in the US after finishing their degrees, and replace the current lottery system with a wage-based selection process that prioritises the highest-paid applicants.

## What the Bill Would Change

Under current law, H-1B holders can apply for employer-sponsored green cards while working in the United States. The queue for Indian nationals is notoriously long — often stretching beyond a decade — but the legal pathway exists, and for many it is the only route to permanent settlement.

Roy's legislation would end that pathway entirely. All H-1B applicants would be required to demonstrate that they maintain a residence abroad and do not intend to abandon it. This would reverse the longstanding principle of "dual intent," which has allowed visa holders to work in the US while simultaneously pursuing permanent residency.

"For its nearly forty-year history, the H-1B visa has been abused, allowing employers to routinely sideline American STEM workers in favour of cheap foreign labour, while masking layoffs and wage suppression as 'shortages,'" Roy said in a statement announcing the bill. "It's time to end this lottery-based pipeline and replace it with a system that prioritises merit, enforces real wage standards, and puts American white-collar workers first."

The bill would also require employers to certify that no qualified American worker is available before sponsoring an H-1B petition, and would bar companies that have recently conducted layoffs from hiring foreign workers through the programme.

## Why This Matters for the Indian Diaspora

Indians are by far the largest beneficiaries of the H-1B programme, accounting for over 70 percent of approved petitions in recent years. The visa has been the primary vehicle through which Indian engineers, doctors, and technology professionals enter the American workforce. Eliminating the green card pathway would fundamentally alter the calculus for anyone considering a career in the United States.

The elimination of OPT would be equally disruptive. The programme allows foreign students graduating from US universities to work for up to three years in STEM fields after completing their degrees. It has served as a critical bridge between education and long-term employment for tens of thousands of Indian students each year. Without it, many would have no legal way to gain work experience in America after graduation.

## The Broader Context

Roy's bill arrives at a moment of maximum turbulence for Indian workers in the US immigration system. Just days ago, a federal judge struck down the Trump administration's $100,000 fee on H-1B applications, ruling it an unlawful tax that Congress never authorised. The ruling was cheered by diaspora advocacy groups, but the administration has signalled it will appeal.

Meanwhile, the State Department moved the EB-2 India green card priority date backward by 10 months in the June visa bulletin, pushing thousands of applicants further from the finish line.

The bill faces long odds in a Congress consumed by other priorities, and immigration advocates note that similar proposals have been introduced before without gaining traction. But its introduction reflects a hardening political consensus around restricting skilled immigration — one that neither party's leadership has shown much appetite to resist.

For the roughly 600,000 Indian nationals currently in the H-1B queue, and the thousands of students arriving each year with plans to build careers in America, the message from Capitol Hill is getting harder to ignore: the ladder you climbed may not be there much longer.

**Sources:** IANS reporting (June 6), Travel and Leisure Asia (June 8), The Hindu / Ease My Prep analysis, Nagaland Post, MySandesh
